A.explanation: This is the volume that supports only $2.00\text{ N}$, the probe and string weight alone, ignoring the $5.00\text{ N}$ weight of the sphere.

B.explanation: This is the volume that supports $3.00\text{ N}$, the difference of the two weights, but equilibrium needs the sum of the downward forces.

C.explanation: This is the volume that supports only $5.00\text{ N}$, the sphere weight alone, ignoring the extra $2.00\text{ N}$ pull from the hanging probe and string.

D.explanation: This is the volume that gives an upthrust of $7.00\text{ N}$, balancing the sphere weight plus the probe and string weight.

hints: Notice the sphere is in equilibrium while pulling up the $2.00\text{ N}$ probe and string, so the water must support both the $5.00\text{ N}$ sphere and the hanging load.
For floating equilibrium, upward upthrust on the submerged part of the sphere equals total downward weight, and upthrust equals $\rho g V$ with $\rho = 1.03 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$.
Add the weights to get total downward force, then rearrange $V = F / (\rho g)$ and check that your volume is near $7 / 10100 \approx 6.9 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^3$.
walkthrough: Identify the forces on the floating system. Downward are sphere weight $5.00\text{ N}$ and tension from the probe and string $2.00\text{ N}$. Upward is upthrust $U$ on the submerged part of the sphere only.
Use equilibrium for the stationary sphere: resultant force is zero, so $U = 5.00 + 2.00 = 7.00\text{ N}$.
State Archimedes principle for the sphere: $U = \rho g V$, where $V$ is the volume below the sea surface, $\rho = 1.03 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Calculate denominator $1.03 \times 10^3 \times 9.81 \approx 1.01 \times 10^4\text{ N m}^{-3}$, then $V \approx 7.00 / 1.01 \times 10^4 \approx 6.93 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^3$ with unit $\text{m}^3$.
This matches the value $6.93 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^3$. This is option D
